title: Pupillometry in the Emergency Room For Evaluation, Control and Treatment of Coma of Unknown Etiology
summary:
A large proportion of patients who are presented to emergency rooms have a disturbance of consciousness that cannot be attributed to events such as cardiac arrest/resuscitation or trauma and is therefore usually initially unclear. This condition is called impaired consciousness or coma of unknown etiology (CUE). Disorders of consciousness can be qualitative (disruption of the contents of consciousness) or quantitative (disruption of alertness), or both; the most severe form of quantitative disturbance of consciousness is coma, a state of non-awakenability. These conditions can be persistent or temporary. The causes of CUE can be very different. In a study at a large German university hospital with a constant presence of neurologists in the emergency room, 23% found epileptic seizures, 21% cerebral hemorrhages and 18% intoxications as the three most common causes. Diagnosing the cause of an initially unclear disorder of consciousness is a significant challenge. In the above-mentioned study, this was achieved with full diagnostic effort and the presence of neurologists in a university emergency room - ultimately in 88%. The suspected diagnosis that the rescue service and emergency doctor(s) make BEFORE admission to the emergency room about the underlying cause of CUE only corresponds to around 60% with the final diagnosis and does not correlate with the probability of death, in contrast to the final diagnosis . Despite numerous attempts to systematically triage this condition, the situation remains unsatisfactory.

This study examines the significance of the parameters collected in a technically carried out “quantitative” pupillometry with regard to the diagnoses ultimately made. This is important because, in a second step, technically simple pupillometry could be used in the preclinical phase and could significantly improve the direction of patients to suitable clinics.

interventions.name:
Inclusion of Patients with coma who present to the emergency department

The study will collect data from automated pupillometry at the time of admission to the emergency department as well as routine clinical data, imaging data, and other additional examinations during the visit of the emergency

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
quantitative impairment of consciousness (Glasgow Coma Svale Score < 15), QP performed within 3 hours of admission, inclusion under emergency criteria possible
Exclusion criteria:
Eye injury or known eye disease, death on admission or within 3 hours after admission, impossibility of further diagnostic clarification (e.g. transfer to another clinic before a definitive diagnosis is made)
